chapter.title: Set the pace

cards.body: The best hiking guide you'll ever follow is the one who keeps stopping. On the hike you're leading, your voice sets the pace: how fast you go, how loud, and where you rest. **The rest stops are where people catch up**, so a talk with no pauses is a hike where the leader never once looks back.
cards.simpler: The best hiking guide is the one who keeps stopping. When you give a talk, you are leading a hike, and your voice sets the pace: how fast you go, how loud you are, and where you rest. **The rest stops are where people catch up**. A talk with no pauses is like a hike where the leader never once looks back.

cards.prompt: You're leading six friends up a hill. The path turns steep and rocky. What does a good guide do here?

options.text: Speed up to get the hard bit over with
Slow down, then stop at the top of the steep bit so everyone catches up
Keep exactly the same speed the whole way, to be fair

whyNot.a: That's rushing, not leading: the steep part is where people fall behind, so speeding up loses them.
whyNot.c: That's a metronome, not a guide: one even speed treats the easy stretch and the hard stretch as the same.

cards.reteach: On a hike, steep bits need a slower pace and a stop at the top. In a talk, the steep bits are the new or important ideas. Slow down there and pause after, so listeners can catch their breath.

cards.title: Speed and the pause
cards.body:
Your listeners can't rewind you. A reader can glance back up the page; a listener gets each sentence once, at the speed you choose.

So **slow down where the idea is new**, and move a little quicker through what they already know, like the set-up of a story. The change of speed is itself a signal: it tells the room *this bit matters*.

The pause is your strongest tool. Three seconds of silence feels like a minute to you. To the room, it feels like a bench at a viewpoint: time to take in what you just said.
cards.simpler: Listeners can't rewind you. A reader can look back up the page, but a listener hears each sentence once, at your speed. **Slow down where the idea is new**, and go quicker through what they already know, like the set-up of a story. Changing speed tells the room this matters. The pause is your strongest tool. Three seconds of quiet feels like a minute to you. To the room, it's a bench at a viewpoint, a rest to take it in.

cards.title: One sentence, three ways
cards.body: Priya is pitching a new rota to her team of 9. Her key line: "We'll stop working Saturdays from March." First try, she says it at the same speed as the line before it, and two people keep reading their phones. Second try, she pauses before it, slows right down on *stop working Saturdays*, then waits 3 full seconds. Someone at the back says "wait, really?", which is the best review a sentence can get.
cards.simpler: Priya is pitching a new rota to her team of 9. Her key line is: "We'll stop working Saturdays from March." First time, she says it at the same speed as the line before, and two people keep reading their phones. Second time, she pauses before it, slows right down on *stop working Saturdays*, then waits 3 full seconds. Someone at the back says "wait, really?" That's the best review a sentence can get.

cards.prompt: Sam has 5 minutes to argue his café should open at 7am, not 8. Which plan uses pace well?

options.text: Say the whole talk quickly so it fits easily into 4 minutes
Slow down on "we turn away 40 people before 8", then stay silent for 3 seconds
Pause after every single sentence so each one gets a rest stop

whyNot.a: That's racing to the summit, not leading: finishing early doesn't help if the room fell behind on the key number.
whyNot.c: That's stopping every ten steps, not resting at the steep bits: when pauses are everywhere, none of them stands out.

cards.reteach: Pace isn't about the clock; it's about where the listener needs time. Find the one line that carries your idea, slow down on it, then stay quiet long enough for it to land. Everywhere else, keep walking.

cards.title: The quiet line
cards.body:
Speed has two partners. *Volume* is how loud you are; *pitch* is how high or low your voice sits. You'd think louder grabs a room. Often a quieter line pulls people in more, like a guide who whispers "look, a deer".

That whisper works a bit like a pause: everyone slows down and leans in. **Dropping your voice on the key line is another way to say *stop here*.**
cards.simpler: Speed has two partners: volume (how loud) and pitch (how high or low). A quiet line often pulls people in, like a guide whispering "look, a deer". The whisper works a bit like a pause: everyone slows down and leans in. **Dropping your voice on the key line is another way to say *stop here*.**

cards.body: Tom has a Monday update and he's nervous, so he talks faster, filling every gap with "um" and "so, yeah". He finishes 90 seconds early, relieved, and then his manager asks a question he answered in minute two. Here's how to spot it: if you finished early and nobody caught your main point, you rushed it. **Nerves speed you up; a planned pause is how you take the pace back.**
cards.simpler: Tom is nervous about his Monday update, so he talks faster and fills every gap with "um" and "so, yeah". He finishes 90 seconds early, relieved. Then his manager asks a question he already answered in minute two. Here's the sign: if you finished early and nobody caught your main point, you rushed. **Nerves speed you up; a planned pause is how you take the pace back.**

cards.prompt: What is a pause in a talk mainly for?

options.text: Giving the listener time to take in what you just said
Giving you time to remember your next line
Showing the room you're calm and confident

whyNot.b: That's a side benefit for the speaker, not the job: the pause is a rest stop for the people walking behind you.
whyNot.c: That's how a pause can look, not what it's for: it exists so the listener can catch up.

cards.reteach: Listeners can't scroll back. A pause is the moment their brain finishes your last sentence before the next one arrives. Put it right after the line that matters most: it's there for them, not you.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Pace is for the listener: **slow down on what's new, and pause after the line that matters** so they can catch up. A quieter voice on that line can do the same job.
cards.simpler: Pace is for the people listening: **slow down on what's new, and pause after the line that matters** so they can catch up. Saying that line more quietly can help too.

cards.body:
Open your phone's voice recorder. Say your talk's one-idea sentence three times: fast, then slow, then slow with a 3-second pause before the key word. Play them back. Which one would a stranger remember?

Tomorrow: why the scariest part of a talk is the bit you didn't plan.
cards.simpler: Open the voice recorder on your phone. Say the one sentence that sums up your talk, three times: first fast, then slow, then slow with a 3-second pause before the key word. Play all three back. Which one would a stranger remember? Tomorrow: why the scariest part of a talk is the bit you didn't plan.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now say the same sentence 3 ways and hold a 3-second pause on purpose.

repairedFrom.why: The volume, pitch and warm-up card wanders off pace: Julian Treasure's seven habits are about what you say, not how fast you say it, and none of the exercises test this card.
repairedFrom.fix: Cut the Julian Treasure paragraph and the warm-up from card 6 and keep only the whispered 'look, a deer' line as a pace tool, then drop 'warm up your voice in 2 minutes' from the outcomeLine and move the 'Tomorrow:' line to the end of the try card so the chapter's last line is the hook for the next chapter.
